summary: Discovery focused on Elk Ridge's expected traffic bursts for model serving, required tenant isolation levels, and encryption/KMS needs. Redwood AE/SE covered Dedicated capacity options, warm pool vs. on-demand burst, failure modes, and an initial pilot plan (72-hour spike sim). Action items include pricing, SOC2/KMS docs, and a simulated spike run.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-11 16:00 PT | 48 mins | Attendees: Jenna (Redwood AE), Omar (Redwood SE), Marta (Elk Ridge), Luis (Infra), Harpreet (Security)

[00:00:07] Jenna Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Jenna with Redwood, and with me is Omar from our solutions engineering team. Quick round robin?
[00:00:15] Marta Chen: Hi all, Marta here. Head of ML at Elk Ridge. We're evaluating options for predictable inference cost and handling spikes from model retrains and batch conversions.
[00:00:24] Luis Vega: Luis, infra. I'll be doing the integration for any VPC or private deployment.
[00:00:29] Harpreet Singh: Harpreet — security lead. I have questions around KMS, audit logs, and data residency.
[00:00:35] Jenna Park: Great. Goal today is to understand your burst patterns, isolation needs, and what success looks like. We'll cover dedicated reserved pools, warm/prewarm strategies, and private path if needed.

[00:01:10] Omar Ruiz: Quick clarifier — when you say "spikes from retrains", are these synchronous user-facing requests or large async batch jobs that generate a lot of inference load?
[00:01:20] Marta Chen: It's a mix. We have user-facing scoring for our analytics UI that will spike during morning digest times, and then larger internal batch scoring jobs after model trains which can be heavy for a few hours. So two classes of load.

[00:02:05] Jenna Park: Could you give us some numbers — QPS, token counts, percentiles you care about?
[00:02:12] Marta Chen: Baseline is like 50 qps for small models during the day. Spikes can hit 600-800 qps for short windows, maybe 15-30 minutes, and then we have afternoon batch runs that are sustained for 2-3 hours at 400 qps. Token lengths are variable — UI calls are small, 16-64 tokens, batch jobs average 512 tokens.

[00:03:02] Omar Ruiz: Okay that delta is significant. For Dedicated we typically size pools for steady-state plus a warm pool for burst. Warm pool keeps KV cache and reduces cold start latency. For 800 qps spikes you likely want a combination of prewarmed nodes and autoscale headroom.

[00:03:40] Luis Vega: Can you explain warm pool vs. just scaling up more nodes? Our concern is eviction and multi-tenant "blast radius" — we run other teams on the same project.
[00:03:49] Omar Ruiz: Sure. Warm pool means nodes kept idle but with model weights loaded and KV cache possibly primed — so warm-up latency is low. If you scale up from zero you pay cold-start penalty and it can take minutes to load weights especially for larger models. Warm pool costs more baseline but reduces tail latency during spikes.

[00:04:30] Marta Chen: How does Redwood isolate workloads? We need strong tenant isolation for IP and compliance.
[00:04:37] Jenna Park: For Dedicated customers we offer tenant isolation options: single-tenant node pinning, tenant fencing (soft isolation via cgroups + scheduler caps), and private on-prem/VPC where you control networking. Single-tenant nodes are the strongest isolation but costlier.

[00:05:10] Harpreet Singh: From a compliance standpoint, we need audit trails and KMS integration. Does Redwood support customer-managed keys?
[00:05:18] Omar Ruiz: Yes — for Private and Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS. For Hosted, we have a managed KMS but can support customer-managed keys via external HSM in private deployments. We'll send the KMS integration checklist after the call.

[00:06:05] Marta Chen: There's also egress concerns — we need traffic to stay inside our VPC when on private deployment. Is that supported?
[00:06:11] Jenna Park: Yep. Private installs can be deployed into your VPC with no public egress. We'll coordinate with Luis on network peering, NAT rules, and any firewall ports.

[00:06:55] [00:06:55] Luis Vega: Quick question — what happens if a warm pool node fails in the middle of a spike? We can't have retries blowing past SLA.
[00:07:03] Omar Ruiz: If a node fails we have automatic fallback routing to another pool or a lower-cost compatible model variant. We also support prewarmed spare nodes for redundancy. There's a tradeoff — more spares increases cost but reduces single-point shock.

[00:07:40] Marta Chen: How configurable are eviction policies? We might accept eviction for non-critical jobs but not for customer-facing scoring.
[00:07:47] Omar Ruiz: Eviction policies are per-queue and per-tenant. You can mark job classes as critical (never evict) or best-effort (evictable). We can integrate with your scheduler or use Redwood's routing policies to enforce that.

[00:08:30] Harpreet Singh: Audit logs — retention windows, where are logs stored?
[00:08:36] Jenna Park: For Dedicated we can ship logs to your S3-compatible bucket or to your SIEM. Retention is configurable; standard is 90 days but extendable. We provide request-level tracing for inference calls and token-level cost breakdowns.

[00:09:20] Omar Ruiz: Let's talk numbers for warm-pool sizing. Based on 800 qps peaks and your token lengths, a rough starting point is N dedicated nodes for steady 50 qps plus M warm nodes to absorb 80% of peak — so you only autoscale the last 20%. What kind of GPU types do you prefer — A100s, H100s, or something quantized on L40s?
[00:09:48] Marta Chen: Right now we run mixed infra. Training uses H100 on-prem, but inference cost optimization means we want to use quantized models on L40-class or A100. We don't have strict hardware lock-in, but cost matters.

[00:10:20] Luis Vega: Do you support mixed model variants — like a faster lower-quality fallback during spikes?
[00:10:26] Omar Ruiz: Absolutely. Smart routing can fallback to a smaller or quantized variant automatically when capacity is constrained, preserving availability while degrading fidelity gracefully.

[00:11:05] Marta Chen: What's the typical latency for a warm node vs a cold start for a 13B-ish model?
[00:11:11] Omar Ruiz: Warm node p95 for 13B is usually sub-200ms per call for short sequences; cold-start to load weights can be tens of seconds to a minute depending on disk cache and model size. That's why warm pool is important for user-facing latency.

[00:12:00] Harpreet Singh: On encryption at rest — we need all model artifacts and caches encrypted under our KMS keys. Is that possible?
[00:12:06] Jenna Park: Yes, with Private deployments we can encrypt model weights and cache under your customer-managed KMS/HSM. For Hosted we have options but some controls require Private. We'll send the exact matrix.

[00:12:45] Omar Ruiz: Operational question — do you have SLA targets for 99th percentile latency or cost per 1k tokens?
[00:12:52] Marta Chen: Stakeholders want p99 under 500ms for UI scoring and predictable unit cost under $0.10 per 1k tokens for non-real-time batch. There's some flexibility.

[00:13:30] Omar Ruiz: We'll align model variants and batching to hit those numbers. For p99 under 500ms we usually need prewarmed nodes plus small batching windows. Batching helps for cost but increases tail latency if you're not careful.

[00:14:20] Luis Vega: For the private path, what's the time to deploy an on-prem instance? We have change windows and we need a minimal maintenance window.
[00:14:27] Jenna Park: On-prem path timeline varies — small proof-of-concept can be provisioned in 2-4 weeks, full production private deployments usually 6-10 weeks depending on procurement and network approvals. We can run a hosted Dedicated pilot to reduce time to value while parallelizing private setup.

[00:15:10] Marta Chen: Would you recommend starting with hosted dedicated or go straight to private?
[00:15:16] Omar Ruiz: Many customers start with Hosted Dedicated to validate workload and cost, then migrate to Private for stronger controls. Given your compliance needs, a parallel track (pilot hosted while prepping private) seems sensible.

[00:16:05] Harpreet Singh: We need SOC 2 and pen test artifacts before any production PII flows.
[00:16:11] Jenna Park: Understood — we'll attach our SOC 2 Type II summary and redacted pen test overview. For private/on-prem we can provide on-site audit support if needed.

[00:17:00] [00:17:00] Marta Chen: About scaling expectations — if the batch job pattern is sustained 2-3 hours at 400 qps, is autoscaling able to maintain cost-efficiency? We don't want to buy double steady-state for that window.
[00:17:10] Omar Ruiz: Autoscaling works but depends on how fast you need capacity. If the batch is predictable, schedule-based prewarmed nodes are more cost-effective. For unpredictable spikes, a blend of minimal warm pool + quick autoscale + fallback model variant reduces cost while protecting availability.

[00:18:00] Luis Vega: Any constraints around Kubernetes namespaces or our internal scheduler? We prefer to keep infra ownership.
[00:18:06] Omar Ruiz: For Private deployments you can host Redwood runtime in your Kubernetes cluster and control namespaces. For Hosted Dedicated we run the runtime but provide RBAC and tenant-level controls. We'll map options for each path.

[00:19:00] Marta Chen: Let's talk pilot scope — what would a realistic pilot look like?
[00:19:06] Jenna Park: Pilot: 2-week Dedicated hosted trial with baseline steady nodes + warm pool sized for your typical spikes, run the 72-hour synthetic spike sim, instrument metrics and unit economics, and a security review for SOC2/KMS. That should give data to decide private.

[00:19:55] Omar Ruiz: For the 72-hour sim we'll ask for a week of your traffic traces and a sample batch job script. We'll replay at real timing to capture tail behaviors.

[00:20:30] Harpreet Singh: We'll need an NDA addendum for sensitive traces.
[00:20:34] Jenna Park: Noted — I'll attach an addendum template.

[00:21:10] [00:21:10] Marta Chen: One more thing — how do you handle model rollouts and KV cache priming so a new model doesn't cause a cold start spike?
[00:21:18] Omar Ruiz: We support canary rollouts with staged traffic and cache priming. You can also pre-load weights in the warm pool and run a short priming job to populate KV cache before ramping traffic. We have hooks to orchestrate that with your CI.

[00:22:05] Luis Vega: What's the telemetry surface we get? Token-level cost, latency heatmaps?
[00:22:11] Jenna Park: Yes — you get token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency distributions, model-level throughput charts, and traces we can forward to your APM.

[00:23:00] Marta Chen: Any gotchas we should be aware of?
[00:23:05] Omar Ruiz: Watch out for anti-patterns: too-large batching for interactive routes, not priming KV cache for new models, and under-provisioning warm pool versus latency SLOs. Also, quantization can occasionally change output distribution — include quality checks in rollouts.

[00:24:00] Harpreet Singh: Where do we sign up for the pilot contract and what's the pricing ballpark?
[00:24:06] Jenna Park: I'll send a pilot quote — ballpark for your expected profile (steady 50 qps, warm-pool for 600-800 qps spikes) is in the mid-five-figure monthly range for Dedicated hosted pilot including warm pool. Exact numbers in the spreadsheet.

[00:24:50] Marta Chen: Sounds good. If the pilot shows cost savings we'll push for dedicated private.

[00:25:20] Omar Ruiz: Cool — next, any networking constraints we should know about? Ports, firewall, private link?
[00:25:28] Luis Vega: We prefer PrivateLink and limited egress. We'll provide network contacts.

[00:26:05] Jenna Park: Noted. We'll include PrivateLink/peering options in the follow-up.

[00:27:00] [00:27:00] Marta Chen: Timeline — we'd like to have pilot data within 3 weeks and a decision by end of month. Is that feasible?
[00:27:06] Omar Ruiz: Tight but doable if we get traces and approvals this week. Pilot kickoff within 5 business days after the paperwork.

[00:28:00] Harpreet Singh: Security checklist items we'll expect: SOC 2, IP handling, KMS integration docs, pen test summary, log forwarding capabilities.

[00:28:10] Jenna Park: We'll provide all of those.

[00:29:00] Marta Chen: Any mention of competitor behavior here? We've had calls with PylonAI — they wanted us to buy upfront for peak.
[00:29:07] Jenna Park: Right, we've seen that. Our approach is more flexible — pilot hosted dedicated then private, with warm pool and fallback variants to avoid huge upfront commits.

[00:30:00] Omar Ruiz: Technical deep dive note — if you want, we can run an initial lightweight profiling run to estimate cache hit rates and batching benefits before the pilot.

[00:30:20] Luis Vega: Please do.

[00:31:00] [00:31:00] Marta Chen: Ok let's recap next steps — Jenna pricing, KMS/SOC docs; Omar sim and profiling; Harpreet provide KMS contacts; Luis network contacts.
[00:31:12] Jenna Park: Correct. I'll get the pricing and NDA addendum out today and the warm-pool spreadsheet by Wednesday. Omar will start on the sim configuration once we have traces.

[00:32:00] Harpreet Singh: One more compliance ask — do you support Bring Your Own Key across warm pool caches as well as model artifacts? We need proof.
[00:32:08] Omar Ruiz: Yes for Private. For Hosted Dedicated we'll outline what is supported today and what requires Private. We'll include a matrix in the doc.

[00:33:00] Marta Chen: Perfect. Anything else?
[00:33:06] Luis Vega: No, that's it from infra.
[00:33:10] Jenna Park: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and a proposed pilot start date.

[00:33:30] [00:33:30] End of call"
